name: Nut Brown
lede: Nut brown is the brown of nuts, in practice a warm reddish brown; it is among the most common browns in our painting archive.

sections.title: A hazelnut's brown
sections.body:
The Dictionary of Colour says nut brown is often the reddish brown of the hazelnut but, strictly, a general brown used for the many shades of nuts [1]. It is also one of the names in a brown series in the introduction to Baty's study of naturalists' color lists, between tombac brown and liver brown [2]. The swatch here is a dark, warm brown. Close neighbors are [[chestnut]], [[cocoa]] and [[hazel]], and the lighter [[russet]] [6].

Another nut gave brown its darker cousin. The English word maroon was originally nut brown, from the French *marron*, chestnut, and now means a brownish dark red [3]. See [[chestnut]].

sections.title: Kola nut and indigo
sections.body: Nuts are also real dye sources. A classic West African color combination pairs indigo with kola nut brown, and Balfour-Paul writes that it is sadly dying out [4]. Compare [[sepia]] and [[umber]], browns that come from other sources.

sections.title: A color of weather and wood
sections.body: The artist Derek Jarman remembers old women with weather-beaten nut-brown faces, in a passage about the nostalgia of brown [5].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
This is one of the most common colors in our archive: it appears in 3,889 of 23,781 paintings, 16.35 percent, more common than 96 percent of named colors, as photographed [6]. Inside a painting it most often plays a mid-tone, in 32 percent of the 2,249 paintings where it is measured [6]. It peaks in the 1500s, in 301 of 2,231 paintings (13.5 percent), about 1.5 times the expected rate [6]. The earliest matches are medieval, but the archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a floor, not a first [6].

The most devoted painter is Maarten van Heemskerck, who uses it in 7 of his 12 works here, about 4.5 times the baseline [6]. It is most over-represented in Tibetan paintings, 3.4 times expected (10 of 47) [6]. It shares canvases with [[cocoa]] more than chance (lift 3.0) [6]. In printed English the word peaks in the 1800s [6].
